events.title: Anticipatory Action Plan (AAP) for Riverine Floods – Southwest Region Cameroon
events.summary: Country: Cameroon Sources: Christian Blind Mission, Presbyterian Church, Welthungerhilfe Please refer to the attached file. This plan by WHH Anticipatory Humanitarian Action Facility (WAHAFA) partners Christian Blind Mission (CBM) and the Presbyterian Church in Cameroon (PCC) shows how Anticipatory Action supports flood-prone communities in Limbe, Fako Division, Cameroon, to act before severe riverine flooding occurs. This locally developed Anticipatory Action Plan (AAP) combines rainfall forecasts and community observations to trigger early actions addressing health risks, property damage, displacement and food insecurity. Developed with communities, local authorities and organizations of persons with disabilities, the AAP includes drainage clearance, early warning communication and the distribution of water purification tablets, hygiene supplies, mosquito nets and food items. Using a two-phase trigger mechanism based on forecasts from the National Observatory on Climate Change (ONACC) and local observations of soil saturation, the AAP enables the activation of anticipatory actions with a lead time of approximately 3-9 days and the release of pre-agreed finance from the WAHAFA Fuel funding.

events.summary: Countries: Ethiopia, Kenya Source: Islamic Relief Almost 700,000 people have been displaced amid an escalation of conflict in southern Ethiopia along the Kenya, Somalia, Ethiopia border as aid agencies prepare to respond, Islamic Relief says. The fighting began on 22 October between Somali and Oromo communities, two ethnic groups living in Ethiopia. The epicentre of the conflict is Moyale a border town projected to be increasingly wealthy as trade grows between Kenya and Ethiopia with the two groups fighting for land. The conflict has spread up to 300km from the town with fighting breaking out in areas across the ethnic group settlements. Approximately 329,000 people have been displaced from the Somali Region Dawa Zone and 359,798 people were displaced across Southern Oromia. Access to the locations has been challenging but aid agencies have had reports that a humanitarian response is necessary. Hundreds of thousands of displaced people will need support before they can return to their homes. The conflict has caused the destruction and burning of homes, businesses and fuel stations, significant disruption of health, nutrition, water and sanitation services; and civilians are vulnerable to attack. Approximately 50,000 people have crossed the Ethiopian border into Kenya seeking safety and humanitarian assistance placing additional pressure on local services and host communities. Islamic Relief Ethiopia head of programmes, Kedir Musema Hameza said: “This is a volatile conflict driven by two ethnic groups competing for land and wealth in the borders of Ethiopia. events.title: World toilet day 2026 - Safe toilets, equal futures
events.summary: Countries: World, Ethiopia, Mozambique, Somalia, South Sudan, Yemen Source: International Organization for Migration Please refer to the attached file. World Toilet Day 2026 focuses on the connection between sanitation and gender equality. Access to safe, private and dignified toilets is essential to protecting the health and safety of women and girls, supporting their education and livelihoods, and enabling their full participation in society. Sanitation is foundational to gender equality. By the end of 2025, 82.2 million people were living in internal displacement within their own countries (IDMC, 2026). Many live in camps and informal settlements where sanitation facilities are shared, overcrowded or inadequate. For displaced women and girls, the lack of safe toilets can affect their daily routines, mobility and access to education and livelihood opportunities. The sanitation crisis affects everyone, but not equally. Unsafe sanitation exposes women and girls to diseases, danger and abuse. In displacement-affected communities, communal toilets without functioning locks, adequate lighting or sex-segregated facilities can compromise privacy and expose women and girls to heightened protection risks, including gender-based violence. Safe sanitation is a universal human right, and safe toilets mean equal futures. Everyone should have access to sanitation facilities that are safe, accessible, private, inclusive and responsive to their needs. This requires not only appropriate infrastructure, but also meaningful community participation, effective management and regular maintenance. events.title: Afghanistan: Afghan women call for greater opportunities at Global Open Day with SRSG Fatima | United Nations Peace Operations
events.summary: Country: Afghanistan Source: UN Assistance Mission in Afghanistan KABUL - Afghan women leaders, journalists, entrepreneurs and civil society representatives met with the Special Representative of the Secretary-General and Head of UNAMA, Rabab Fatima, during a United Nations-supported Global Open Day event in Kabul, calling for greater opportunities and meaningful participation for women in Afghan society. The event brought together around 50 women's rights advocates, media representatives, business leaders, and community members to discuss the challenges facing Afghan women and girls and exchange ideas on how to address them. In her remarks, Fatima commended the contributions of Afghan women. "Across the country, I have seen the determination, contribution and leadership of women," she said, emphasising that women do not want to be passive recipients of support but active participants in shaping the decisions and policies that affect their lives. Participants stressed the importance of ensuring women's meaningful participation in public life, including access to education, employment and other fundamental rights. Their calls come amid continued restrictions on women and girls. As of 2026, an estimated 2.4 million girls remain excluded from secondary education, reversing two decades of progress in expanding access to learning opportunities. "What will happen to Afghanistan in 20 years without educated women?" asked one participant. Launched by the United Nations Security Council in 2010, Global Open Day events are held worldwide to promote dialogue between United Nations representatives and women's organizations, raise awareness of women's contributions to peace and security, and support their participation in conflict prevention and resolution.

events.summary: Country: Somalia Source: UN Children's Fund Please refer to the attached file. Highlights Somalia's humanitarian needs remained high during the quarter, driven by drought, conflict, displacement, disease outbreaks and declining humanitarian assistance. An estimated 5.1 million people faced acute food insecurity (IPC Phase 3+), while 1.92 million children were projected to suffer acute malnutrition between July 2026 and June 2027. About 75,000 displacement movements and over 1,400 conflict events were recorded. UNICEF sustained lifesaving assistance across priority sectors, reaching 98,241 children with SAM treatment, 244,022 caregivers with IYCF counselling, 145,671 people with primary health care, and 286,006 people with safe water. Education support benefited 71,644 children, while 48,991 people accessed child protection services. Monthly cash transfers supported 13,493 vulnerable women, strengthening household resilience. The 2026 Humanitarian Action for Children (HAC) appeal was 27 per cent funded (US$32 million) against US$121 million required, leaving a US$89 million gap. Underfunding continued to constrain service coverage, operational capacity and emergency preparedness for anticipated El Nino impacts.

Armed violence escalated sharply across the globe in 2025. Data from the Uppsala Conflict Data Program (UCDP) shows that conflict-related fatalities rose to 244,600, up from approximately 187,000 in 2024. This made 2025 one of the deadliest years since the end of the Cold War. Much of the increase was driven by a dramatic rise in violence targeting civilians, particularly in Sudan. While armed conflict affects entire populations, children are among those who suffer the most severe and lasting consequences. Children face grave violations , including killing and maiming, recruitment by armed groups, sexual violence, abduction, attacks on schools and hospitals, and denial of humanitarian access. Children living in conflict-affected areas are more likely to drop out of school, lack access to clean water, and face heightened risks of death from illness, malnutrition, or lack of vaccines and medical care. UNFPA warns: the world risks letting the next generation down A mix of economic instability, inequality, exclusion and other destabilizing factors are holding young people back from fulfilling their ambitions. New York, 19 November 2026 — Young people have never been more educated, connected to information or aware of their rights. Yet for millions, the building blocks of adult life — a decent job, financial independence, a home, relationships, family and a say in their future — are becoming harder to secure. The 2026 State of World Population report, Succeeding Generations: Empowering young people to chart the future , published today by the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA), reveals a growing disconnect between the opportunities young people have gained on paper and the realities they face as they enter adulthood. Many young people are coming of age amid economic insecurity, conflict, climate change, rapidly changing technologies and widening inequality. For some, independence, partnership and parenthood are being pushed later and later. For others, poverty and crisis force adult responsibilities far too soon. events.title: oPt: Beyond Compliance: Strengthening Environmental, Social, Governance and Technical Assurance in Fragile Contexts for Accountable Delivery and Sustainable Impact (Project Insight Note #17)
events.summary: Country: occupied Palestinian territory Source: International Water Management Institute Please refer to the attached file. Wasudha Abeyrathna, Umar Liaqat, Stephen Fragaszy, Vidhisha Samarasekara Abstract/Description This Project Insight Note (PIN) shares lessons from the Al Murunah project’s pilot in Palestine, led by the International Water Management Institute (IWMI) and implemented with the Palestinian Hydrology Group (PHG), on strengthening environmental, social and governance (ESG) and technical assurance for physical works in fragile and conflict-affected settings. It describes a layered assurance approach that includes early partner due diligence, a living ESG risk register, multidisciplinary technical and safeguards reviews, quantity and cost verification, virtual field trips, and an independent engineering review when site access was lost. The PIN shows that ESG oversight works best when it is built into project design and followed through with corrective action and sustainability planning, helping to build trust and support the scaling of climate resilience investment.

November 17, 2026 New York and Brussels – The United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) and the European Union (EU) have launched a new phase of their partnership on Insider Mediation (2026-2029), expanding support for local peacebuilders working to prevent violence, resolve disputes and build lasting peace in conflict-affected communities. Building on the achievements of the previous phase (2023-2026), the renewed partnership will strengthen the capacity of insider mediators to respond to emerging tensions and support locally-led peacebuilding. A key feature of the new phase is a rapid response mechanism that will provide flexible funding and technical assistance, enabling mediators to act quickly when tensions arise or opportunities for dialogue emerge.
